paragraphs: Airbnb began because its founders could not afford San Francisco rent. In October 2007, Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia put air mattresses on their apartment floor and rented them to attendees of a design conference who had found every hotel in the city booked, charging eighty dollars a night and calling it Air Bed and Breakfast.

A third founder, Nathan Blecharczyk, joined to build the website, and the site formally launched in August 2008. Investors turned the pitch down repeatedly; the founders famously kept the company afloat partly by selling novelty cereal boxes branded for the 2008 election. It later grew into a marketplace covering millions of listings worldwide.

John Alcock and Arthur Brown took off from a field near St John's, Newfoundland, on 14 June 1919 in a converted Vickers Vimy bomber, chasing a 10,000-pound prize the Daily Mail had offered years earlier for the first nonstop transatlantic flight. Brown had to climb out onto the wings mid-flight, without a parachute, to chip ice off the engines by hand.

Sixteen hours later they crash-landed nose-first into a bog near Clifden, Ireland, both men unhurt, having beaten a scheduled airliner route by decades. Their arrival came less than a month after American aviators had crossed the Atlantic with refuelling stops, which is why Alcock and Brown's flight, rather than that one, is remembered as the nonstop first.

The earthquake struck Antioch on the morning of 13 December 115, while Emperor Trajan was wintering in the city partway through his campaign against Parthia. Trajan was trapped inside a collapsing building and escaped through a window with only minor injuries; the consul Marcus Pedo Vergilianus, who was staying with him, was killed in the same collapse.

Estimated at around magnitude 7.5, the quake devastated Antioch along with the nearby resort of Daphne and several other cities in the Orontes valley, and ancient estimates put the dead at roughly 260,000 out of a population near half a million. Trajan and his successor Hadrian, who survived the same disaster as a young officer, both funded reconstruction, though parts of the city were abandoned outright.

Apple introduced the Macintosh on 24 January 1984 at a shareholders' meeting in Cupertino, two days after airing the Ridley Scott advertisement that had run once, during the Super Bowl, and cost more per second than most companies spent on a whole campaign. The machine itself sold for 2,495 dollars and shipped with 128 kilobytes of memory, tight even by the standards of the day.

It borrowed its windows-and-mouse interface directly from what Apple engineers had seen demonstrated at Xerox PARC five years earlier, and though early sales were respectable they fell well short of Apple's own forecasts once the novelty wore off. Steve Jobs was pushed out of the company he had co-founded within about eighteen months of the launch he had staged so theatrically.

Soviet planners began diverting the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers into unlined irrigation canals starting around 1960, aiming to turn the arid plains of Central Asia into cotton fields regardless of what fed the inland sea downstream. The Aral had been the world's fourth largest lake, and it received almost no replenishment once the canals were running at scale.

By the early 2000s the sea had split into separate, shrinking basins and lost roughly 90 percent of its former volume, stranding fishing towns like Moynaq dozens of kilometres from any shoreline, their boats left rusting on dry sand. Kazakhstan later rebuilt a dam that partly restored the smaller northern basin, but the larger southern Aral has continued to retreat into desert.

The first atomic clock, built at the National Bureau of Standards in 1949, did not use the caesium atoms that define time today. It used ammonia molecules, which vibrate at a fixed rate that can be measured with a microwave signal, giving a timekeeping standard tied to a property of matter rather than the swing of a pendulum or the vibration of a quartz crystal.

It was less accurate than the best pendulum clocks already running, so it worked as a proof of concept rather than a working standard. Caesium clocks replaced ammonia within a few years and became precise enough that the second itself was redefined in 1967 using caesium's oscillation instead of the Earth's rotation.

Beethoven never called it the Moonlight Sonata. He titled the piece Quasi una fantasia, a sonata in the manner of a fantasy, and dedicated it to a young countess he had been giving piano lessons. The nickname came five years after his death, coined by a critic who thought the opening movement recalled moonlight over Lake Lucerne.

That first movement, slow and quiet, was itself unusual: sonatas of the period almost always opened fast. Beethoven composed the piece around 1801, as his hearing was starting to fail, though the connection between the two is guesswork rather than anything he wrote down. The nickname outlived the dedication; few remember the countess's name today.

Franklin described the idea in an August 1784 letter, complaining that carrying two pairs of spectacles to Paris, one for reading and one for the theatre across the room, meant constantly swapping them. His solution was a single lens cut in half, with the distance prescription set in the upper part of the frame and the reading prescription in the lower.

He never patented the design or wrote it up as an invention in any formal sense; the letter to a friend is the only documentary evidence historians have. Franklin was in his late seventies at the time, serving as American minister to France, and the split-lens idea he mentioned in passing became the standard bifocal still ground the same way today.

Concorde's first flight, on 2 March 1969 from Toulouse, carried no passengers at all. It was a 29 minute test flight of the French-built prototype, still well below the speed of sound; the aircraft would not break Mach 1 until October that year and would not enter airline service for another seven.

The programme was a joint venture between France and Britain, built to a shared design so neither government could cancel its half alone. Only twenty aircraft were ever built, and just fourteen entered commercial service, cutting the London to New York crossing to about three hours before rising costs and a fatal 2000 crash ended flights in 2003.

Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson were not looking for evidence of the Big Bang in 1965. They were trying to eliminate noise from a radio antenna at Bell Labs in New Jersey, and after ruling out interference and even cleaning out pigeon droppings from the horn, a faint, uniform hiss remained no matter which direction the antenna pointed.

A team at nearby Princeton, led by Robert Dicke, had predicted exactly this kind of leftover radiation from an early hot universe and was building equipment to detect it when they heard about the Bell Labs signal. The two groups published companion papers; Penzias and Wilson received the 1978 Nobel Prize for a discovery they had first mistaken for a fault in their equipment.

Victoria Gray, a mother of four from Forest, Mississippi, received an infusion of her own gene-edited cells in July 2019 as part of a clinical trial run by Vertex and CRISPR Therapeutics. Doctors had removed her bone marrow stem cells, used CRISPR to switch on a fetal haemoglobin gene that normally shuts off after birth, and returned them to her body.

Gray had lived with sickle cell disease since childhood, with pain crises severe enough for repeated hospital admissions. The edited cells took hold, and her symptoms largely disappeared. The therapy, later named Casgevy, won FDA approval in December 2023, becoming the first CRISPR-based treatment cleared for use outside a trial.

The Cuyahoga had caught fire more than a dozen times since the 1860s, thick enough with industrial oil and debris to burn, and the June 1969 fire that made national headlines was actually smaller and shorter than several earlier blazes on the same river through Cleveland. No photograph of the 1969 fire itself is known to survive; the image later used in Time magazine's coverage was from a more dramatic 1952 fire.

Timing mattered more than scale: the story broke just as a national environmental movement was gathering, and it became a shorthand for industrial pollution more broadly. Congress passed the Clean Water Act in 1972, and the river has since recovered enough that fish species considered wiped out decades earlier now spawn in stretches that once had almost no oxygen to sustain them.

NTT DoCoMo switched on the world's first commercial 3G network in Japan on 1 October 2001, branded FOMA, using a technology called W-CDMA that had been under development through the 1990s. Early adoption was slow: handsets were expensive and coverage was limited to Tokyo and a handful of other cities at launch.

The jump mattered because earlier mobile networks were built for voice calls and struggled to move data faster than a dial-up modem. 3G raised that ceiling enough to support video calls, web browsing and, eventually, the app-based smartphones that followed once similar networks reached other countries over the next several years.

Gerhard Domagk tested Prontosil on his own daughter before he published anything about it. In 1935 the child had a severe infection from a needle prick, and with no approved treatment available, Domagk gave her the red dye he had been trialling on infected mice. She recovered, and he wrote up the drug's results the same year.

Prontosil itself did not kill bacteria in a test tube; it only worked inside a living body, because the body broke it down into an active compound called sulfanilamide. That discovery opened the sulfa drug era, treatments that predated penicillin's wide use by nearly a decade and cut death rates from infections like childbed fever sharply.

James Clerk Maxwell is remembered for equations, not cameras, but in 1861 he demonstrated to the Royal Institution that colour could be captured by photographing the same object three times through red, green and blue filters, then projecting the three black-and-white negatives back together through matching filters.

The subject was a tartan ribbon, chosen because its pattern showed colour separation clearly. The photographic plates of the day were barely sensitive to red light at all, so the result was duller and less accurate than Maxwell intended, yet the three-colour principle behind it is still the basis of colour photography and television screens today.

Thomas Parker had already made his name electrifying tramways and, later, part of the London Underground when he built one of the earliest practical electric cars in Wolverhampton in 1884. He ran the Elwell-Parker company there with Paul Bedford Elwell, manufacturing the lead-acid accumulators and dynamos that made a battery-powered carriage feasible rather than a novelty that died after a mile.

Steam and, soon after, petrol dominated the roads that followed, and Parker's car remained a workshop achievement rather than a commercial product line. He is nonetheless recorded in what is thought to be the earliest surviving photograph of anyone driving an electric car, seated in his own vehicle on a Wolverhampton street before the decade was out.

George Beauchamp had been trying to make a Hawaiian-style lap steel guitar loud enough to hold its own against a dance band, and by 1931 he and machinist Adolph Rickenbacker had built a cast aluminium prototype nicknamed the Frying Pan because of its round, skillet-shaped body and long neck. A horseshoe-shaped magnet wrapped around the strings turned their vibration into an electrical signal.

Beauchamp and Rickenbacker formed the Ro-Pat-In Corporation, later Rickenbacker, and put the Frying Pan into production in 1932 as the Electro A-22, sold alongside a matching amplifier since neither device was any use without the other. It was built for steel guitar, not the standard six-string players would later plug in, but the pickup design underneath it became the template for the electric guitar industry that followed.

IBM Simon went on sale to the public on 16 August 1994 for around 900 dollars with a two-year contract. It had no name recognisable as a phone brand behind it and no app store, but it packed a touchscreen, a calendar, a notepad, and an email client into a slab the size of a brick, years before anyone used the word smartphone.

IBM sold roughly 50,000 units before pulling it from shelves the following February. The battery lasted about an hour, and the stylus was easy to lose. Simon vanished from most people's memory for a decade, resurfacing only after the iPhone made a touchscreen phone with software seem like a new idea rather than a repeated one.

Neil Papworth, a 22-year-old test engineer for Sema Group, typed 'Merry Christmas' on a computer keyboard and sent it over Vodafone's network on 3 December 1992 to a colleague's Orbitel 901 handset. The phone itself had no keyboard capable of sending a reply; texting only worked one way until handsets caught up.

SMS had been specified years earlier as a minor feature riding along inside the GSM standard, intended mainly for network alerts rather than person-to-person chat, and phone makers were slow to build a way to type messages on a handset at all. It took most of the 1990s for texting to become a habit rather than a curiosity, and by the following decade it was generating more revenue for carriers than voice calls in some markets.

Gary Thuerk worked in marketing at Digital Equipment Corporation, and on 3 May 1978 he sent a single message announcing a new line of VAX computers to nearly every address on ARPANET's west coast, roughly 400 accounts out of the network's 2,600 users at the time. There was no rule against it because nobody had imagined the problem yet.

Recipients complained immediately, and a network manager reprimanded Thuerk for breaking ARPANET's rules against unofficial use. Thuerk later claimed the mailing generated millions of dollars in sales for DEC. The term spam for unwanted bulk messages did not attach itself to email until well over a decade later, borrowed from a Monty Python sketch.

The game was not yet called the Super Bowl. The programme and most newspapers called it the AFL-NFL World Championship Game, and it was played before a stadium that was barely half full: 61,946 people at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, which seats over 90,000, on 15 January 1967.

Green Bay beat Kansas City 35 to 10. Quarterback Bart Starr threw two touchdown passes and was named the game's first MVP, but the score was close at half time before the Packers pulled away. The name Super Bowl only became official from the third edition, once Kansas City owner Lamar Hunt's nickname for it, borrowed from his children's rubber ball, stuck.

Architect and information designer Richard Saul Wurman convened the first TED in February 1984 at the Monterey Conference Center, betting that technology, entertainment and design belonged in one room together. The bill included an early demonstration of the Apple Macintosh and of the Sony compact disc, plus a talk from mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot on the fractals he had spent a decade formalising.

It lost money and was not repeated for six years; Wurman did not hold a second TED until 1990, and the conference only became an annual fixture from 1992. The now-familiar format, eighteen-minute talks streamed free online to millions, arrived later still, once Chris Anderson's nonprofit took over in 2002 and put the archive on the web from 2006.

Finland, then an autonomous grand duchy inside the Russian Empire, had granted women full voting and standing rights in 1906, and in the elections held in March 1907 nineteen women won seats in the new unicameral Eduskunta out of two hundred members. It was the first parliament anywhere in the world to seat women elected under universal suffrage.

The nineteen came from across the political spectrum, from the Social Democrats to the conservative parties, and included Miina Sillanpaa, who had started work in domestic service as a child and went on to become Finland's first female government minister in 1926. Other countries followed at very different speeds: Norway seated a woman in 1911, but the United Kingdom's Westminster Parliament did not until 1919.

OpenAI published the paper behind the first GPT model in June 2018, describing a system trained by first learning general language patterns from a large body of unlabelled text and only afterward being tuned for a specific task. That two-stage approach, not the model's size, was the part other researchers picked up and built on almost immediately.

The original GPT had 117 million parameters, a figure that looks almost quaint against the models that followed within a few years. OpenAI did not treat it as a finished product; each successor was trained on more text and released with less caution, culminating in the decision to withhold GPT-2's full training data over misuse concerns the first version had never raised.

Dean Kamen built his first infusion pump while still an undergraduate, working out of his parents' basement, and founded a company called AutoSyringe in 1976 to manufacture it. The device was wearable rather than implanted, letting a patient carry a mechanical pump that delivered measured doses instead of relying on scheduled injections.

The pump was adopted well beyond diabetes care, used for chemotherapy and newborn medicine as well as insulin delivery, because the underlying problem, a drug that needed steady dosing rather than a single jolt, was the same across specialities. Kamen sold AutoSyringe to Baxter Healthcare and went on to found DEKA Research, later known for the Segway.

On the morning of 20 November 1980, a Texaco crew drilling for oil beneath Lake Peigneur in Louisiana missed its mapped position by around 400 feet and punched straight into an active salt mine working underneath the lake bed. Water began pouring into the mine shafts, and the resulting whirlpool grew large enough to swallow the drilling rig, eleven barges and a good chunk of the surrounding shoreline.

The lake, previously about ten feet deep and fresh, drained entirely into the mine within hours and refilled as a saltwater lake roughly 200 feet deep, briefly reversing the flow of the canal that connected it to the Gulf of Mexico. Nobody died: the mine's crew had time to evacuate, and nine of the sunken barges eventually popped back to the surface once the crater stabilised.

Windows 95 went on sale on 24 August 1995 after a launch event with Jay Leno and a licensing fee reportedly paid to the Rolling Stones for the use of Start Me Up as its advertising jingle. Retailers in some cities opened at midnight, and customers queued for a piece of software the way they had previously queued for concert tickets.

The technical leap was a Start button and taskbar that made switching between programs simple, plus support for long file names and plug-and-play hardware. Underneath, it still leaned on MS-DOS code for compatibility, a compromise that would linger in Windows for years. Microsoft sold an estimated seven million copies in the first five weeks.

The MP3 was not named or standardised in a single moment; the German Fraunhofer Institute team, led by Karlheinz Brandenburg, had been refining the compression method through the 1980s, and the format only took its familiar .mp3 file extension in 1995, after years spent as MPEG Audio Layer III inside a broader video standard.

Brandenburg reportedly used a recording of Suzanne Vega's song Tom's Diner to fine-tune the algorithm, listening for artefacts a compressed file introduced into a single, mostly unaccompanied voice. The format shrank songs to roughly a tenth of a CD track's size, small enough to trade online, which is exactly what made it the engine of music piracy in the years that followed.

Nintendo tested the NES in New York City in 1985 rather than launching it nationally, wary after the 1983 crash that had left American retailers unwilling to stock any home console. To get around that reluctance, Nintendo dressed the machine up as something other than a games console: a front-loading cartridge slot styled like a VCR, a plastic robot toy, and a light gun packaged in.

The gamble worked. By the time the console rolled out across the rest of the country in 1986, Super Mario Bros. was already bundled with it, and American toy stores that had sworn off video games two years earlier were reordering stock. The industry Atari had nearly killed off was, within a couple of years, bigger than it had ever been.

Netflix added streaming as a free extra for existing DVD-by-mail subscribers on 16 January 2007, with a library of about a thousand titles, mostly older films and television, that could be watched through a web browser on a computer. There was no separate charge and no expectation yet that streaming would outgrow the mail-order business funding it.

For years the DVD service brought in far more revenue than streaming did, and Netflix kept mailing red envelopes long after most subscribers had stopped opening them. Streaming only overtook DVD revenue around 2011, the same period Netflix began commissioning its own original series rather than licensing everything it showed.

Two German hikers, Erika and Helmut Simon, spotted a body melting out of glacial ice on a mountain path in the Ötztal Alps on 19 September 1991. Rescuers at first assumed it was a recent mountaineering casualty, one of the dozens the region loses each year, and hacked at the ice with pickaxes before anyone realised the corpse belonged to someone far older.

Radiocarbon dating placed Ötzi's death at roughly 3300 BC, making him Europe's oldest known naturally preserved mummy. He carried a copper axe, a bow, and arrows, and an arrowhead lodged in his shoulder shows he was killed rather than dying of exposure, a mystery still argued over by the researchers who have studied his remains ever since.

The original locks, opened in 1914, could not fit the largest container ships built by the 2000s; those vessels, sized to the canal's own limits, were nicknamed Panamax. The expansion, approved by a 2006 referendum and finished a decade later on 26 June 2016, added a third, wider lane with locks roughly 70 metres wide against the original 33.

The project cost about $5.25 billion and ran over its original schedule, partly because of disputes with the construction consortium over unexpected costs. The new locks reuse most of their water through side basins rather than flushing it to the sea, a design meant to reduce the fresh water each transit consumes.

The documents did not come from a government raid or a court order. An anonymous source calling themselves John Doe sent 11.5 million files, roughly 2.6 terabytes, to the German newspaper Suddeutsche Zeitung, all drawn from the internal records of a single Panamanian law firm, Mossack Fonseca, that specialised in setting up offshore companies.

The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists coordinated reporters across more than 75 countries before publishing in April 2016. The fallout reached sitting leaders directly: Iceland's prime minister resigned within days, and Pakistan's Nawaz Sharif was later disqualified from office over assets the leak had traced to his family.

By 1786 the cemetery of Les Innocents in central Paris had been used for burials for roughly ten centuries and was overflowing so badly that a cellar wall on an adjoining street collapsed under the pressure of decomposing bodies. The city government ordered the remains moved at night, by torchlit cart, into the exhausted limestone quarries that already honeycombed the ground beneath the Left Bank.

The transfer of bones ran on and off for about two years and eventually filled several kilometres of tunnel with the remains of an estimated six million people. In 1810 the quarry inspector Louis-Etienne Hericart de Thury had the bones arranged into the walls of skulls and femurs that visitors still walk past, turning a sanitation project into what became one of Paris's stranger tourist sites.

Athens surrendered in 404 BCE after a Spartan fleet under Lysander had already destroyed its navy at Aegospotami the previous year and then blockaded the city until starvation forced terms. The peace stripped Athens of its empire, its fleet down to a token dozen ships, and the Long Walls that had connected the city to its port were torn down while Spartan musicians played.

Sparta installed a puppet government of thirty oligarchs, remembered afterward as the Thirty Tyrants, who ran a brief and violent purge before Athenian democrats overthrew them within a year. The war had run for twenty seven years across two exhausting phases, and it left the balance of power in Greece with Sparta for barely a generation before Thebes and then Macedon displaced it in turn.

The building known as the Treasury was cut directly into a cliff of rose-coloured sandstone rather than built up from a foundation, carved from the top down so scaffolding never had to reach higher than the workers already stood. Scholars still argue over the exact dating, placing it anywhere from around 100 BC to the early first century AD, under the Nabataean kings who controlled Petra's caravan trade in incense and spice.

Bedouin who lived among the ruins centuries later gave it the name Al-Khazneh, the Treasury, believing an urn carved near the top held hidden gold; bullet scars on that urn mark generations of people who took shots at it hoping to crack it open. It was almost certainly built as a royal tomb, not a vault, and no treasure was ever found inside.

Pompeii was found by accident during work at a nearby site, Herculaneum, and the first deliberate digging at Pompeii itself began in 1748 under Rocque Joaquin de Alcubierre, a Spanish military engineer working for the Bourbon king of Naples. His early methods were closer to treasure hunting than archaeology: workers tunnelled toward statues and valuables and left much of the site's context undocumented.

The city had been buried under volcanic ash from Vesuvius in 79 CE, which sealed it so completely that plaster casts made from the voids left by decomposed bodies still show the folds of clothing and the positions people died in. Careful, stratified excavation did not really begin until the 1860s, under Giuseppe Fiorelli, nearly 120 years after Alcubierre's crews first broke ground.

The signal in 1895 travelled barely a mile and a half across the grounds of Marconi's family estate near Bologna, from a transmitter to a receiver his assistant carried. Nobody heard a voice. It was a Morse pulse, and the whole apparatus depended on decades of prior work by Hertz, Tesla and Oliver Lodge that Marconi combined rather than originated.

What Marconi had that the others lacked was patience for the unglamorous part: patents, demonstrations for investors, and a company built to sell the idea before anyone agreed it was useful. By 1901 he had a signal crossing the Atlantic. The move from telegraphy's dots and dashes to an actual broadcast voice took another two decades.

Charles Richter built his scale in 1935 to solve an office problem, not a public one: Caltech's seismological lab was fielding constant press calls asking how big each Southern California tremor had been, and Richter wanted a single number that did not require reading a full seismogram.

The scale is logarithmic, so each whole step up represents roughly thirty times more energy released, and it worked well only for nearby, moderate quakes recorded on a specific instrument. Richter developed the method with his colleague Beno Gutenberg, though Gutenberg's name is largely forgotten; seismologists now use other scales for large or distant earthquakes, but the public still says Richter.

Rinderpest killed cattle, not people, but its outbreaks caused human famines by wiping out the animals that ploughed fields and provided milk; a single 1890s epidemic swept across sub-Saharan Africa and killed an estimated eighty to ninety percent of cattle in some regions, alongside wild buffalo and antelope.

The World Organisation for Animal Health declared the disease eradicated on 25 May 2011, following a decades-long vaccination campaign run jointly with the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. It became only the second disease ever eradicated worldwide, after smallpox, and the first animal disease. No case has been confirmed anywhere since 2001.

J. Howard Miller painted the 'We Can Do It!' poster in 1943 for Westinghouse Electric, and it was never public advertising: it hung inside Westinghouse factories for about two weeks that February as an internal morale piece aimed at discouraging absenteeism and unionised grumbling among women already on the line. It had no connection to the name Rosie the Riveter at the time.

The poster vanished into company files for decades and was rediscovered in the National Archives in the early 1980s, after which it was attached retroactively to the wartime figure of Rosie, a name popularised separately by a 1943 song and a Norman Rockwell magazine cover. Its status as a feminist icon is almost entirely a postwar invention, built from an image nobody saw as one at the time.

Transit 1B went up from Cape Canaveral on 13 April 1960 aboard a Thor rocket, built to solve a narrow problem: Polaris submarines needed to know their exact position before firing a missile, and a periscope star sighting was not precise enough. The satellite broadcast a signal whose Doppler shift, measured as it crossed the sky, let a ship calculate its own location.

It was not usable in real time and not built for civilians; a fix could take the better part of an hour to compute. The Navy ran the system for over thirty years regardless, and the engineers who designed GPS in the 1970s started from Transit's Doppler method before replacing it with the constellation of atomic clocks GPS still relies on today.

The 1597 printing of Romeo and Juliet was not one Shakespeare approved. It is what scholars call a bad quarto, likely pieced together from actors' memories or shorthand notes taken during a performance, full of garbled lines and stage directions that read like someone describing the play rather than transcribing it.

A cleaner text followed in 1599, advertised on its title page as newly corrected and augmented. Shakespeare based the plot on an English poem by Arthur Brooke from 1562, itself translated from an Italian tale, so the feuding families and the poison already existed before he wrote a word. What he added was the language.

Sony released the PlayStation in Japan on 3 December 1994, a product that existed largely because Nintendo had insulted Sony a few years earlier. Sony had built a CD-ROM add-on for the Super Nintendo under a partnership deal, only for Nintendo to quietly strike a rival agreement with Philips and drop Sony entirely.

Sony's engineers kept working on the abandoned hardware and turned it into a standalone console instead of a add-on, built around CDs rather than the cartridges every previous machine had used. It undercut cartridge production costs, courted third-party developers Nintendo had treated as an afterthought, and by the end of the 1990s had sold more than 100 million units worldwide.

Chuck Hull built his first stereolithography apparatus in a lab in California in 1983 and filed the patent in 1984, describing a way to cure liquid resin layer by layer with an ultraviolet laser until a solid object emerged from the vat. He founded 3D Systems soon after to commercialise it, and the first machine reached customers in 1988.

For its first two decades the technology stayed inside industrial design studios, making prototype parts too expensive and too slow for anything else. It only became a household word once patents began expiring around 2009, opening the door to cheap desktop printers built on a different method, fused deposition, that Hull's original process never used.

ARPANET switched over to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983, a date its administrators had been calling flag day for months because every host on the network had to convert simultaneously or lose contact with the rest. The older protocol, NCP, could only address machines directly connected to the original network and had no real way to link separate networks together.

TCP/IP split the job into two layers, one moving packets and one guaranteeing they arrived intact and in order, which meant any network could join as long as it spoke that shared language at the edges. Vint Cerf and Robert Kahn had designed it through the 1970s for exactly that purpose, and the 1983 cutover is the reason the internet is a network of networks rather than one expanding ARPANET.

In March 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an in a drought year hit fragments of clay figures a few feet underground. Yang Zhifa, one of the men digging, later said they thought they had found a kiln god and were unsure whether to be pleased or worried about disturbing it. Archaeologists identified the pieces as part of the buried army of China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang.

Excavation eventually uncovered over 8,000 life-sized soldiers, along with horses and chariots, each face individually modelled rather than cast from a single mould. The farmers received a small reward at the time; decades later, some of them worked at the museum built over the site, signing books for visitors who had come to see what their well-digging turned up.

ByteDance bought Musical.ly, a Shanghai-founded lip-sync app popular mainly with American teenagers, for around a billion dollars in 2017. In August 2018 it merged Musical.ly's user accounts directly into its own short-video app TikTok, migrating tens of millions of existing profiles, videos and followers overnight rather than launching from nothing.

The merger let TikTok skip the years most social platforms need to build an initial audience; it inherited Musical.ly's users and their existing habit of posting short lip-sync and dance clips. Within two years it had been downloaded more than two billion times, a growth curve that drew the scrutiny from US lawmakers that has followed the app since.

On the night of 9 to 10 March 1945, 279 American B-29 bombers dropped incendiary clusters over Tokyo's densely built wooden districts in a raid codenamed Operation Meetinghouse. Flying low to improve accuracy, the bombers ignited a firestorm that outran anyone trying to escape through streets already choked with smoke and collapsing buildings.

Estimates of the dead run from about 80,000 to over 100,000, with roughly a million people left homeless in a single night, figures that remain higher than either atomic bombing that came later that year. The raid was planned deliberately around the city's wooden construction and used napalm-based bombs designed specifically to exploit it, making it, by most counts, the most destructive single bombing raid of the war.

At 5.29am on 16 July 1945, in the New Mexico desert, a plutonium device built by the Manhattan Project detonated on a hundred-foot steel tower and vaporised it. The explosion was equivalent to roughly 21,000 tons of TNT, far beyond what most of the physicists present had predicted, and it fused the desert sand into a green glass now called trinitite.

Robert Oppenheimer later said the test brought Hindu scripture to mind, but at the time his brother recalled him simply muttering that it worked. Three weeks later a bomb built on the same design was dropped on Nagasaki, after a different design, using uranium, was used on Hiroshima on 6 August.

Travis Kalanick and Garrett Camp registered UberCab in San Francisco in 2009 after struggling to find a taxi on a snowy night in Paris the year before. The original idea was closer to a black-car booking app than the mass ride-share service it became: a smartphone request summoned a licensed town car, and the app split the fare automatically.

San Francisco regulators sent the company a cease-and-desist letter in 2010 over the word cab in its name, and Uber dropped it rather than fight the point. The cheaper, driver-owned-car version of the service, UberX, did not launch until 2012, and it was that version, not the original black cars, that spread the company into hundreds of cities.

Voyager 2 had already spent twelve years travelling when it passed within about 4,950 kilometres of Neptune's cloud tops on 25 August 1989, closer to its target than any of the probe's earlier flybys of Jupiter, Saturn or Uranus. Ground controllers were sending commands across a light-travel time of over four hours, so the whole approach ran on instructions written days in advance.

The images sent back showed a storm system nicknamed the Great Dark Spot, roughly the size of Earth, and six previously unknown moons, including Triton with its geysers of nitrogen ice. Voyager 2 has not been matched since: no other spacecraft has visited Neptune, and none is currently funded to. The probe then kept transmitting from interstellar space, still faintly audible to NASA's Deep Space Network decades later.

The Alto that Xerox PARC engineers built in 1973 was never sold to the public: fewer than two thousand were made, mostly for internal use and a handful of universities, and each one cost the company roughly the price of a house. It ran overlapping windows, icons and a three-button mouse years before any of that vocabulary meant anything to a computer buyer.

Xerox's own sales division saw no market in an office machine with no keyboard-only fallback and largely shelved the idea. Steve Jobs and a group of Apple engineers toured the PARC lab in 1979, and what they saw there fed directly into the Lisa and then the Macintosh, so the interface most people now call intuitive was demonstrated first on a computer almost nobody ever got to buy.
